entries.term: not all who wander are lost
entries.note: A common misquotation of a Lord of the Rings poem Bilbo writes about Aragorn, which actually reads 'not all those who wander are lost'.
Never said by [[see:Marie Antoinette]]; [[see:Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] recorded a different princess saying [[equivalent:qu'ils mangent de la brioche]].
What [[see:Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] recorded a French princess saying, the real source of [[equivalent:let them eat cake]].
Falsely credited with [[see:let them eat cake]]; she was a small child when the line was recorded.

entries.term: if you're going through hell, keep going
entries.note: Often credited to [[see:Winston Churchill]] because people want him to have said it.
Attracts many misattributed quotes, listed by the International Churchill Society; he was a Conservative by 15.
Like [[see:Winston Churchill]], someone who has hoovered up many misquotations.
Like [[see:Winston Churchill]], someone who has hoovered up many misquotations.

entries.term: if you're not a liberal when you're 25, you have no heart
entries.note: Attributed to [[see:Winston Churchill]], unlikely since he was a Conservative at 15; Rob first heard it credited to someone else.
Often credited to [[see:Marilyn Monroe]] but said by a Harvard academic whose name fits the story less well.
Wrongly credited with [[see:well-behaved women seldom make history]].
Often credited with sayings about freedom she never said; she was not known for being verbose.
A common misquotation from Snow White; the wicked stepmother actually says [[see:magic mirror on the wall]].
What Snow White's stepmother actually says, commonly misremembered as [[see:mirror, mirror on the wall]].
Collective misremembering, named after [[from:Nelson Mandela]], whose death and funeral people remembered before he died.
Its logo is widely misremembered as having a cornucopia, an example of the [[see:Mandela effect]].
Widely misremembered as Berenstein, an example of the [[see:Mandela effect]].
Encountering something new and then hearing of it again soon; named after the [[from:Baader-Meinhof Group]], which kept cropping up for journalist [[see:Terry Mullen]].
West German militant organisation that gave its name to the [[gave:Baader-Meinhof effect]].
Trying to hide something reveals it more; named after [[from:Barbra Streisand]], whose legal action over an aerial photo of her house made everyone see it.
Measures astronaut space sickness; named after [[from:Jake Garn]], the first sitting US senator in space, who suffered severe motion sickness.
A 19th-century word meaning to eat without appetite, onomatopoeic, like eating daintily or picking, with a diminutive [[see:-le]] ending.
Ending usually diminutive, as Jess notes for [[see:pingle]].
Founder of structural linguistics, the target of the pun 'now I'm not so sure' in Joshua's favourite linguist joke.
Originally a disease caused by too much of one humour, as found in the hosts' anatomy episode on the four humours.
